marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q001.takeaway: The transverse plane through the sternal angle reaches the T4–T5 intervertebral disc and divides superior from inferior mediastinum.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q001.displayText:
The transverse plane through the sternal angle reaches the T4–T5 intervertebral disc and divides superior from inferior mediastinum.

The mediastinum is divided into superior and inferior parts by a transverse plane extending from the sternal angle to the T4-T5 intervertebral disc. The sternal angle lies opposite the T4 vertebra and upper half of T5 in most adults. This plane separates superior from inferior mediastinum and is also a landmark for the superior limit of the pericardium, bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, origin of the arch of the aorta, and the site where the superior vena cava pierces the pericardium to enter the right atrium.
emphasis: The transverse plane through the sternal angle reaches the T4–T5 intervertebral disc and divides superior from inferior mediastinum

rationales.a: T3–T4 lies above the standard sternal-angle plane.
rationales.b: T2–T3 is too high; the plane is conventionally at T4–T5.
rationales.c: T5–T6 is below the landmark plane.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q002.displayText:

The trachea lies in the superior mediastinum.
emphasis: The cervical trachea enters the superior mediastinum before continuing toward the carina

rationales.b: The anterior mediastinum lies between sternum and pericardium and contains mainly loose tissue/thymic remnants.
rationales.c: The middle mediastinum contains pericardium and heart, not the upper thoracic trachea.
rationales.d: The posterior mediastinum is behind the pericardium; trachea remains anterior.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q003.takeaway: The thymus lies in the superior mediastinum, so thymoma is expected in the anterior-superior mediastinal region.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q003.displayText:
The thymus lies in the superior mediastinum, so thymoma is expected in the anterior-superior mediastinal region.

Thymomas are tumors of the thymus and are associated with myasthenia gravis. The thymus occupies the superior and anterior mediastinum.
emphasis: The thymus lies in the superior mediastinum, so thymoma is expected in the anterior-superior mediastinal region

rationales.b: The middle mediastinum is centered on the pericardium and heart.
rationales.c: The posterior mediastinum contains esophagus, thoracic duct and descending aorta.
rationales.d: Inferior mediastinum is not the usual thymic location.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q004.takeaway: The esophagus descends through the posterior mediastinum behind the pericardium.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q004.displayText:
The esophagus descends through the posterior mediastinum behind the pericardium.

The esophagus is present in the posterior mediastinum. It enters the superior mediastinum between the trachea anteriorly and vertebral column posteriorly, then continues inferiorly into the posterior mediastinum, passes through the diaphragm and opens into the stomach. The thymus is in the superior/anterior mediastinum, the ascending aorta is in the middle mediastinum, and the tracheal bifurcation is in the middle mediastinum.
emphasis: The esophagus descends through the posterior mediastinum behind the pericardium

rationales.a: Thymus is located in superior and anterior mediastinum, especially in children.
rationales.b: Ascending aorta is in the middle mediastinum within the pericardial sac.
rationales.d: Tracheal bifurcation is at the sternal-angle plane and is not a posterior mediastinal structure.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q005.takeaway: The source matches left subclavian artery to superior, hemiazygos vein to posterior, phrenic nerve to middle and sternopericardial ligaments to anterior mediastinum.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q005.displayText:
The source matches left subclavian artery to superior, hemiazygos vein to posterior, phrenic nerve to middle and sternopericardial ligaments to anterior mediastinum.

The source explanation gives the correct matching as A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1: left subclavian artery - superior mediastinum; hemiazygos vein - posterior mediastinum; phrenic nerve - middle mediastinum; sternopericardial ligaments - anterior mediastinum.
emphasis: The source matches left subclavian artery to superior, hemiazygos vein to posterior, phrenic nerve to middle and sternopericardial ligaments to anterior mediastinum

rationales.a: This places left subclavian artery in anterior rather than superior mediastinum and misassigns the remaining structures.
rationales.c: This assigns phrenic nerve to anterior and sternopericardial ligaments to posterior, reversing their compartments.
rationales.d: This places the subclavian artery in middle mediastinum and phrenic nerve posteriorly, both inconsistent with their courses.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q006.takeaway: The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q006.displayText:
The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum.

The heart enclosed in the pericardium occupies the middle mediastinum. The middle mediastinum is the broadest part of the inferior mediastinum and contains the pericardium, heart, tracheal bifurcation and corresponding vessels and nerves. Thymus/remnants are in the superior and anterior mediastinum. The posterior mediastinum is bounded posteriorly by the bodies of T5-T12 vertebrae, and its lower border extends more inferiorly than that of the anterior mediastinum.
emphasis: The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum

rationales.b: Thymic remnants are typically in the superior/anterior mediastinum, not middle.
rationales.c: The posterior mediastinum lies against lower thoracic vertebrae, not T1–T4 as the posterior boundary.
rationales.d: The inferior mediastinum extends to the diaphragm in both anterior and posterior divisions; the anterior part does not extend farther.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q008.takeaway: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches in the neck and loops under the right subclavian artery; it does not descend through the superior thoracic aperture as a mediastinal content.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q008.displayText:
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches in the neck and loops under the right subclavian artery; it does not descend through the superior thoracic aperture as a mediastinal content.

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve does not pass through the superior thoracic aperture. It hooks around the right subclavian artery in the neck and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. The source lists structures traversing the thoracic inlet including esophagus, trachea, lung apices with pleura, thymic remnants, brachiocephalic artery, brachiocephalic veins, left common carotid artery, internal thoracic and superior intercostal arteries, first intercostal veins, inferior thyroid veins, left recurrent laryngeal nerve, bilateral phrenic and vagus nerves, sympathetic trunks, first thoracic nerves, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, longus colli and thoracic duct.
emphasis: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches in the neck and loops under the right subclavian artery; it does not descend through the superior thoracic aperture as a mediastinal content

rationales.b: The left common carotid artery ascends through the superior thoracic aperture into the neck.
rationales.c: The cervical sympathetic trunk continues through the aperture into the thorax.
rationales.d: The thoracic duct ascends through the aperture to enter the root of the neck.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q009.takeaway: SVC obstruction causes downward anterior chest-wall collaterals; the SVC enters the right atrium near the fourth intercostal space but reaches the pericardium near the second costal cartilage, making the third-cartilage statement false.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q009.displayText:
SVC obstruction causes downward anterior chest-wall collaterals; the SVC enters the right atrium near the fourth intercostal space but reaches the pericardium near the second costal cartilage, making the third-cartilage statement false.

The clinical finding is superior vena cava obstruction. The false statement is that the superior vena cava pierces the pericardium at the third costal cartilage. The source places pericardial penetration opposite the second costal cartilage/angle of Louis at the T4-T5 plane. The azygos vein joins about 2 cm below the sternal plane at T5, and the superior vena cava enters the right atrium at the level of the fourth intercostal space. SVC obstruction can cause swelling of the face/neck, dyspnea, headache, dizziness, hemoptysis, dilated neck veins, proptosis, papilledema and prominent anterior chest-wall collateral veins with downward flow.
emphasis: SVC obstruction causes downward anterior chest-wall collaterals; the SVC enters the right atrium near the fourth intercostal space but reaches the pericardium near the second costal cartilage, making the third-cartilage statement false

rationales.a: The SVC opens into the right atrium, so this option is true.
rationales.c: The SVC enters the heart at approximately the fourth intercostal space, matching this option.
rationales.d: The azygos vein joins the SVC below the sternal-angle plane, so this relation is not the false statement.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q010.takeaway: The thoracic duct usually begins at the cisterna chyli around L1–L2 before ascending through the aortic hiatus.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q010.displayText:
The thoracic duct usually begins at the cisterna chyli around L1–L2 before ascending through the aortic hiatus.

The thoracic duct usually originates at the L1 level, anterior to L1/L2. The intestinal trunk and two lumbar lymph trunks join to form the cisterna chyli, which continues as the thoracic duct. The duct enters the posterior mediastinum through the aortic hiatus, lies on the right between the aorta and azygos vein until T4-T5, crosses to the left posterior to the esophagus, ascends and arches over the subclavian artery, and drains into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. It drains both halves of the body below the diaphragm and the left half of the head/neck, left upper limb and left thorax above the diaphragm.
emphasis: The thoracic duct usually begins at the cisterna chyli around L1–L2 before ascending through the aortic hiatus

rationales.b: T7 is in the thorax and is not the usual abdominal origin.
rationales.c: L4 is below the common cisterna chyli origin level.
rationales.d: T11 is above the abdominal origin and not the usual level.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q011.takeaway: The right bronchomediastinal trunk normally drains to the right lymphatic duct/right venous angle rather than the thoracic duct.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q011.displayText:
The right bronchomediastinal trunk normally drains to the right lymphatic duct/right venous angle rather than the thoracic duct.

The thoracic duct does not receive the right bronchomediastinal lymphatic trunk; that trunk contributes to the right lymphatic drainage. The source describes the right lymphatic duct as draining the right half of the body above the diaphragm through the right jugular trunk, right bronchomediastinal trunk and right subclavian trunk. It also notes that thoracic-duct obstruction can cause chylothorax, with obstruction below T5 tending to produce a right pleural effusion and obstruction above T5 a left pleural effusion.
emphasis: The right bronchomediastinal trunk normally drains to the right lymphatic duct/right venous angle rather than the thoracic duct

rationales.a: The lumbar trunks contribute lymph from lower limbs and abdomen to the thoracic duct.
rationales.b: The descending lumbar trunks are also thoracic-duct tributaries in the source classification.
rationales.c: The left upper intercostal trunk drains to the thoracic duct.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q012.takeaway: The thoracic duct terminates at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins (left venous angle).
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q012.displayText:
The thoracic duct terminates at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins (left venous angle).

The fluid shown is chyle, indicating chylothorax from thoracic-duct obstruction. The thoracic duct normally drains into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. Gastric-cancer metastasis to the left supraclavicular Virchow node can mechanically obstruct the thoracic duct near its venous termination and produce a left-sided chylous effusion.
emphasis: The thoracic duct terminates at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins (left venous angle)

rationales.a: The duct does not enter at the SVC–brachiocephalic junction.
rationales.c: The thoracic duct drains into systemic venous circulation, not directly into coronary sinus.
rationales.d: Azygos vein is not the normal thoracic-duct termination.

marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q013.takeaway: The cross-section is at T3–T4, where the aortic arch and its three major branch openings are visible.
marrow__ANAT_CH43_Q013.displayText:
The cross-section is at T3–T4, where the aortic arch and its three major branch openings are visible.

The section is at T3-T4. It shows the large vascular opening of the aortic arch together with the openings of its three major branches: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery. At T1-T2/T2-T3 only smaller branch-vessel openings are expected, while the T4-T5 plane is where the arch begins/ends and the pulmonary trunk bifurcation is visible.
emphasis: The cross-section is at T3–T4, where the aortic arch and its three major branch openings are visible

rationales.a: T1–T2 is too high to show the full arch and its three branch origins.
rationales.b: At T2–T3, the arch branch openings are not all seen at this plane.
rationales.d: T4–T5 is near the arch transition and pulmonary trunk bifurcation rather than the section with all three branch openings.
